newsitem.title: USA: Fed came close to raising rates in September say sources.
newsitem.headline: Fed came close to raising rates in September say sources.

text.p: The Federal Reserve nearly decided to raise short-term interest rates in September and has not shelved that option for the coming months, Fed sources said Tuesday.

"They came very close to raising rates around the time of the September (24) meeting," a Fed source told Reuters, referring to the next-to-last meeting of the policy-setting Federal Open Market Committee.
The source said a number of Fed bank presidents -- such as San Francisco's Robert Parry, the most senior president in the Fed system -- had been favouring a rate rise at the time.
Concern that inflationary pressures would eventually emerge as a result of a tight labour market was the main argument in favour of a rate increase, the source said.
The policy-maker held off from increasing interest rates in what analysts described as a calculated gamble that the economy will slow before inflation starts to rise.

The FOMC meeting was held just days after eight of the 12 Fed district banks requested an increase in the 5.0-percent discount rate, which the Fed charges banks for cash. Three of those banks had sought an increase of half a percentage point.

Another Fed source said Fed Chairman Alan Greenspan had considered, shortly before the September meeting, raising the federal funds rate, which commercial banks charge each other for overnight loans, by half a percentage point to 5.75 percent from 5.25.
That source said Greenspan favoured the 50-basis-point increase in part because a sharp move was more likely to prevent a pronounced selloff in the Treasury bond market.
Central bank officials have expressed sensitivity to Wall Street's reaction, especially in light of the market slump that followed its string of small, gradual rate hikes in 1994.
The possibility of a Treasury market overreaction to a rate change "remains a concern" at the Fed, that source said.
Such concern was highlighted in the minutes of the Sept. 24 meeting, which were released Friday.
"A delay in adjusting monetary policy ... was further supported by the possibility of an excessive reaction in financial markets," the minutes showed.
But the source said a larger rate hike would have required persuasive evidence that a tight labour market was actually feeding through into higher inflation, as they have historically.
Despite an unemployment rate below 5.9 percent since September 1994, few signs of rising inflation are evident.
The source also asserted that financial markets tend to misinterpret the Fed's policy goals.

"The long-term goal remains price stability," the source said, while stressing that the Fed not only remains vigilant against signs of incipient inflation but also aims at driving the underlying inflation trend lower.
The September meeting minutes showed the FOMC maintained the bias toward tightening first put in place at the July 2-3 meeting and sustained after the Aug. 20 meeting.

For the third straight meeting, Minneapolis Fed President Gary Stern dissented from the majority, favouring "modestly more restrictive policy," which Fed-watchers interpreted as an immediate .25-percentage point Fed funds rate hike.
The Fed last met Nov. 13, at which time it left both the Fed funds and discount rates unchanged, as they have been since Jan. 31.
